strings.sec.topire.lead: Bodies can exist in three states of aggregation: solid, liquid and gaseous. Going from one to the other exchanges heat at constant temperature.

strings.top.def1: The passage of a substance from the solid state to the liquid state is called melting.
strings.top.def2: The passage of a substance from the liquid state to the solid state is called freezing (or crystallisation).
strings.top.obs1: melting absorbs heat from the outside, while freezing releases heat to the outside;
strings.top.obs2: during the melting of crystalline substances the temperature stays constant, at a value called the melting temperature; these substances crystallise also at a constant temperature, called the crystallisation temperature, equal to the melting temperature;
strings.top.obs3: amorphous substances (pitch, for instance) have no precise melting temperature: on heating they soften gradually and become more and more fluid as their temperature rises.
strings.top.salt.body: The crystallisation temperature is influenced by dissolved substances. A saturated solution of table salt in water freezes at about −20 °C (the NaCl–water eutectic is at −21.1 °C, for roughly 23 % salt).
strings.top.p1: While a crystalline substance melts, its temperature stays constant. That means the average kinetic energy of the molecules stays constant: the heat received from outside is “spent” entirely on breaking the bonds of the crystal lattice, therefore exclusively on increasing the potential energy of the system of molecules.
strings.top.p2: For this reason the heat received from outside during melting is called latent heat of melting. At the points of segment AB the substance in the solid state coexists with the substance in the liquid state.
strings.top.p3: Melting is a reversible process. Hence, in the reverse process, freezing, the heat released to the outside — called the latent heat of solidification — is equal, in modulus, to the latent heat of melting.
strings.top.p4: where λ_t is the specific latent heat of melting (respectively of solidification), [λ_t] = J/kg, Q is the latent heat exchanged by a mass m of substance, [Q] = J, [m] = kg. The specific latent heat of melting and the melting temperature are quantities characteristic for each substance.
strings.top.demo.title: Demo · the heating curve
strings.top.demo.hint: On the plateau AB you hear a rare “tick”: every tick is a broken lattice bond, not a faster molecule.
strings.ex1511.title: Ice at −10 °C turned into water at 100 °C
strings.ex1511.text: Find the heat Q needed to turn a mass m = 100 g of ice, initially at t₀ = −10 °C, into water at 100 °C. Given: the specific heat of ice c_g = 2090 J/(kg·K), the specific latent heat of melting of ice λ_t = 3.35·10⁵ J/kg and the specific heat of water c_a = 4181 J/(kg·K).
strings.etapa.title: Extension: from ice to steam
strings.etapa.p: The problem above has three stages. If heating continues, two more appear: vaporisation at 100 °C and heating of the steam. The bar below shows what each stage “costs” — you immediately see that the change of state dominates the energy budget.
strings.etapa.note: Values used: c_g = 2090 J/(kg·K), c_a = 4181 J/(kg·K), λ_t = 334 kJ/kg, λ_v = 2.26 MJ/kg at 100 °C, c_steam = 2010 J/(kg·K). Heat losses are neglected.
strings.etapa.demo.title: Demo · heat budget per stage
strings.ano.p1: Usually, because the intermolecular distances grow, the volume of the body increases and, correspondingly, the density decreases. In this case one finds experimentally that: when melting happens at a higher pressure, the melting temperature is higher.
strings.ano.p2: There are exceptions though: ice, bismuth, lead–antimony alloys. For them melting decreases the volume and increases the density (ρ_ice = 917 kg/m³, ρ_water = 1000 kg/m³); when melting happens at a higher pressure, the melting temperature is lower.
strings.ano.p3: From the above it follows that stating the melting temperature of a substance must be accompanied by the pressure at which the melting takes place.
strings.ano.concl.body: The melting and freezing of crystalline substances take place at constant temperature, provided the pressure stays constant.
strings.ano.p4: The slope by which the melting temperature depends on pressure follows from the Clausius–Clapeyron relation. For ice, at 0 °C:
strings.ano.p5: That is, about 130 atm are needed to push the melting point of ice down by a single degree — which is why the ice under skate blades does not melt from pressure, but from friction.
strings.ano.demo.title: Demo · V–t on melting
strings.ano.demo.hint: Raise the pressure and watch which way the plateau moves: up for wax, down for water.
strings.tab.demo.title: Comparative chart
strings.tab.why.title: Why these numbers matter
strings.tab.why1: Melting 1 kg of ice requires about 334 kJ, approximately 160 times the heat needed to warm the same mass of ice by 1 K.
strings.tab.why2: λ_t grows with the lattice energy: mercury (weakly bound metal) melts at −39 °C with 11 kJ/kg, while iron at 1530 °C with 270 kJ/kg.
strings.tab.why3: Silver (960 °C) and iron (1530 °C) appear in the table to compare the temperature scales of everyday metallurgy.
strings.tab.ref.body: Values are rounded and may vary with purity, pressure and temperature. Comparisons are illustrative.
strings.vap.def1: The passage of a substance from the liquid state to the vapour state is called vaporisation.
strings.vap.def2: The passage of a substance from the vapour state to the liquid state is called condensation.
strings.vap.obs1: vaporisation absorbs heat from the outside, while condensation releases heat to the outside;
strings.vap.obs2: When a pure substance boils in equilibrium at constant pressure, its temperature stays constant. Condensation under the same conditions occurs at the same temperature. Surface evaporation also occurs below the boiling temperature.
strings.vap.p1: At the vaporisation temperature the molecules in the liquid have a certain average kinetic energy. Some molecules, however, have a kinetic energy large enough to overcome the cohesion forces and can leave the liquid into the free space above. But, because the liquid is left by the high-energy molecules, the average kinetic energy of the molecules in the liquid decreases and, consequently, the temperature decreases too.
strings.vap.p2: The heat received from outside is “spent” entirely on keeping the temperature — hence the average kinetic energy of the liquid molecules — constant, which ensures the continuity of the vaporisation process. That is why the heat received during vaporisation is called latent heat of vaporisation.
strings.vap.p3: Vaporisation is a reversible process. Hence, in the reverse process, condensation, the heat released to the outside — called the latent heat of condensation — is equal, in modulus, to the latent heat of vaporisation.
strings.vap.p4: The latent heat of vaporisation and the vaporisation temperature are quantities characteristic for each substance. For water λ_v = 2.26·10⁶ J/kg at 100 °C — the largest value among common liquids, which is why sweating cools efficiently and why the sea moderates the climate.
strings.vap.tree.title: how vaporisation is classified
strings.vap.tree.vid: in vacuum — rapid, reaching saturation if liquid remains
strings.vap.kf1.d: only at the surface, at any temperature
strings.vap.kf2.d: throughout the volume, at a fixed temperature
strings.vap.revers.body: The heat absorbed on vaporisation is returned entirely to the environment on condensation: steam heating relies on it and, unfortunately, so do steam burns.
strings.vid.p1: Being less dense, the ether rises to the surface of the mercury in the tube. One finds that the ether vaporises (in vacuum) instantaneously and the mercury level in tube 2 goes down. In tube 3 a slightly larger amount of ether is introduced: the mercury level goes down somewhat more. In tube 4 an even larger amount of ether is introduced — one finds that not the whole amount vaporises any more, and the mercury level goes down further. In tube 5 an even larger amount of ether is introduced: a larger amount remains unevaporised, but the mercury level stays (approximately) the same as in tube 4.
strings.vid.concl1: vaporisation in an initially evacuated chamber can be very rapid;
strings.vid.concl2: vaporisation in vacuum continues until the vapour pressure reaches a maximum value p_m.
strings.vid.p2: When the vapour pressure equals p_m, the vapour is called saturated vapour. In this case the vapour is in equilibrium with the liquid it came from: the height of the ether columns in tubes 4 and 5 does not change in time. That means that, every second, the number of molecules crossing from the liquid into the gas above equals the number of molecules crossing from the gas into the liquid.
strings.vid.def: Saturated vapours are the vapours in dynamic equilibrium with the liquid they come from.
strings.vid.p3: At molecular level, the liquid–saturated-vapour equilibrium is therefore a dynamic equilibrium.
strings.vid.e1: the pressure of the saturated vapours does not depend on the mass of liquid, nor on the mass of vapour in contact with the liquid it comes from;
strings.vid.e2: at constant temperature the pressure of the saturated vapours does not depend on volume: increasing the volume leads to vaporising an extra amount of liquid, and decreasing the volume to condensing some vapour, but the level of the mercury column does not change;
strings.vid.e3: the pressure of the saturated vapours depends on temperature;
strings.vid.e4: at constant temperature, the pressure of the saturated vapours depends only on the nature of the liquid they come from.
strings.vid.why.body: When the temperature rises, the average kinetic energy of the liquid molecules rises too, so more molecules can leave the liquid — the saturated vapour pressure grows. The dependence on the nature of the liquid is explained by the intermolecular (cohesion) forces and by the mechanical work done against their resultant, which are characteristic for each liquid.
strings.vid.dalton.body: In a gas, vapour transport is slowed by diffusion. In the ideal-mixture approximation, saturation vapour partial pressure depends on temperature rather than the presence of non-condensable gases.
strings.vid.demo.title: Demo · Torricelli tubes with ether
strings.vid.demo.hint: Go past the dose that fills the tube: the pressure locks at p_m and liquid stays unevaporised.
strings.vid.echi.title: Demo · dynamic equilibrium
strings.eva.p1: Experimentally one finds that vaporisation (in open air) happens the faster, the larger the free surface of the liquid. This shows that vaporisation (in open air) takes place at the surface of the liquid. This is the phenomenon of evaporation.
strings.eva.f2: the speed of evaporation grows when the temperature grows;
strings.eva.f3: during evaporation the temperature of the liquid decreases.
strings.eva.p2: At a higher temperature the average kinetic energy is larger. Therefore the number of molecules whose kinetic energy is large enough to cross the surface layer of the liquid, doing work against the intermolecular forces, is larger, so the evaporation speed is larger. But even at low temperatures, when the average kinetic energy is smaller, there are molecules (fewer of them) with enough kinetic energy to leave the liquid.
strings.eva.p3: The molecules which leave the liquid during evaporation have kinetic energies larger than the average kinetic energy. That is why, in the course of evaporation, the average kinetic energy falls and, correspondingly, the temperature of the liquid falls.
strings.eva.cool.body: It is the same mechanism behind sweating, the ground cooling after rain and the formation of mist. A thermometer with its bulb wrapped in wet cotton shows the “wet-bulb” temperature, always lower than the air temperature.
strings.eva.demo.title: Demo · evaporative cooling of water
strings.eva.demo.hint: Illustrative model for 50 g of water: vaporisation removes heat while the 300 K surroundings supply heat. Area and wind are relative parameters; the mass flow is not an experimental measurement. The model stops at freezing or when the water is exhausted.
strings.fie.p1: Heating water can first release dissolved air bubbles. These alone do not prove boiling. Vapour bubbles can grow within the liquid when their pressure can balance the local pressure; the hydrostatic contribution is neglected in this shallow-vessel model.
strings.fie.p2: Pure water boils at approximately 100 °C at normal atmospheric pressure. At fixed pressure, further supplied heat vaporises the water without increasing its temperature. A different pressure gives a different boiling temperature.
strings.fie.safe.body: For the practical activity use a needle-free syringe and room-temperature water. Do not heat the syringe. Handle the heated vessel and heat source according to laboratory rules.
strings.fie.f1: at a given pressure, each liquid has a characteristic boiling temperature, constant during boiling;
strings.fie.f2: the boiling temperature of a liquid grows when the external pressure grows;
strings.fie.f3: the boiling of a liquid starts when, by raising the temperature, the pressure of its saturated vapours becomes equal to the external pressure exerted on the free surface of the liquid.
strings.fie.obs.body: Pure water boils, at normal atmospheric pressure, at 100 °C. At a pressure of 10 atm it boils at 180 °C, while at a pressure of 4.5 torr it boils at 0 °C.
strings.fie.demo.title: Demo · heating and boiling in a syringe
strings.fie.demo.hint: Choose the experiment above. In Heating mode, start the burner and observe the temperature rise followed by a plateau. In Syringe mode, pull the plunger and observe the pressure drop and temporary bubbles; push it back to stop boiling.
strings.fie.st.fierbe: Boiling — constant temperature at fixed pressure
strings.ex1521.title: A water drop inside an evacuated enclosure
strings.ex1521.text: A water drop at approximately 0 °C is placed in an evacuated chamber. In an adiabatic model, what fraction f freezes as the remainder vaporises? Use λ_g = 334 kJ/kg and λ_v = 2.50 MJ/kg. Neglect heat exchange with the vessel and subsequent sublimation.
strings.psat.demo.title: Demo · p_sat(T) for water
strings.psat.demo.hint: Reference points: approximately 4.6 torr at 0 °C, 760 torr at 100 °C and 10 atm at 180 °C. The Antoine curve is an approximation.
strings.faze.def1: The passage of a substance from the solid state directly into the vapour state is called sublimation.
strings.faze.def2: The passage of a substance from the vapour state directly into the solid state is called desublimation.
strings.faze.obs.title: Observations:
strings.faze.obs1: Snow and ice sublime, going directly into vapour. That explains how frozen laundry dries in winter.
strings.faze.obs2: Iodine and camphor can pass from solid to vapour. A solid material’s smell may come from volatile components without the entire material subliming.
strings.faze.p1: The points on the curves represent states in which the substance coexists in two states of aggregation (for instance solid – liquid). The three curves meet in a single, common point. That point represents a unique state in which the substance coexists in all three states of aggregation. Hence the point is called the triple point, and the unique state it represents is called the triple state.
strings.faze.p2: This state, for the ice–water–water-vapour system, was chosen as the reference state for defining the absolute temperature and was conventionally assigned the temperature 273.16 K.
strings.faze.p3: For water, the melting curve slopes left: ice occupies more volume than liquid water, so pressure favours melting. For most substances the curve slopes right.
strings.faze.p4: If the external pressure is smaller than p_tr, the liquid cannot exist: on heating, the solid goes directly into vapour. This is the case of carbon dioxide („dry ice”, which sublimes at −78.5 °C at atmospheric pressure) and, partly, of frozen wet clothing.
strings.faze.demo.title: Demo · the phase diagram
strings.faze.demo.hint: Bring the pressure below 611 Pa and raise the temperature: the ice no longer melts, it sublimes directly.

strings.boil.protocol.title: The syringe experiment, step by step
strings.boil.protocol.1: Draw about 5 mL of room-temperature water into a transparent, needle-free syringe. Expel large air bubbles and close the outlet with a suitable cap.
strings.boil.protocol.2: Pull the plunger: the space above the water expands and pressure falls. If the total pressure becomes sufficiently low, vapour bubbles can grow even at room temperature.
strings.boil.protocol.3: Hold the plunger in place. Newly formed vapour raises pressure in the sealed chamber, while vaporisation consumes energy and slightly cools the water. Boiling weakens and stops; pressure does not stay fixed at its minimum.
strings.boil.protocol.4: Push the plunger back. Pressure rises, some vapour condenses and boiling stops. Compare this with heating at fixed pressure: the syringe has no burner.
strings.boil.scale.note: The graph shows calculated values; the syringe uses a detailed vertical scale because cooling can be small.
strings.boil.note: Illustrative model: pure water, ideal gas headspace and latent heat exchange. The syringe contains 5 mL of water at 25 °C; headspace increases from 0.2 to 20 mL, then pressure is recalculated as vapour forms. Cooling can be small; the graph uses a detailed scale. Values are calculated, not measured. Heating runs four times faster; the syringe uses 1:1 simulated time. The vessel contains 100 g of water and maximum heater power is 800 W. For the syringe, piston work and heat transfer through the walls are neglected.
strings.boil.graph.title: Temperature versus time
strings.eva.rate.title: Evaporation rate — mass flow rate
strings.eva.rate.definition: The average evaporation rate is the net mass of liquid evaporated per unit time. The instantaneous rate is given by the decrease in liquid mass:
strings.eva.rate.units: Δm_ev is the evaporated mass, Δt the time interval and m_l the remaining liquid mass. The SI unit is kg/s; the simulation displays g/s: 1 g/s = 10⁻³ kg/s. This measures the rate of mass loss.
strings.eva.rate.dalton: An empirical Dalton-type relation describes dependence on surface area and vapour-pressure deficit:
strings.eva.rate.symbols: S is the free-surface area [m²], p_sat(T) the saturation pressure at the liquid-surface temperature [Pa] and p_v the vapour partial pressure in the air [Pa]. The coefficient k, in kg/(m²·s·Pa), depends on airflow, atmospheric pressure, temperature and geometry.
strings.eva.rate.interpretation: A larger surface and drier air favour evaporation. At p_v = p_sat(T), net flow is zero; if p_v exceeds p_sat(T), condensation occurs. This relation is approximate; the demonstration uses an illustrative rate and relative parameters without experimentally calibrating k.
strings.model.limits: Schematic model: pure-substance equilibrium, approximate saturation curves and neglected heat losses. High-pressure ice phases are excluded.
strings.sec.lichefiere.title: Gas liquefaction. Andrews isotherms
strings.sec.lichefiere.lead: How can a gas become liquid? Explore isothermal compression, liquid–vapour coexistence and the limit set by critical temperature.
strings.home.map.9: Gas liquefaction, Andrews isotherms and the critical point
strings.liq.intro: Liquefaction is the change from gas to liquid. To achieve it by isothermal compression, temperature must be below the critical temperature T_c. Heat must be removed during compression; otherwise the gas warms and the process is not isothermal.
strings.liq.andrews.title: What Andrews isotherms show
strings.liq.andrews.intro: Thomas Andrews studied carbon dioxide under compression at constant temperature. An isotherm gives pressure versus volume for a fixed amount of substance at one temperature.
strings.liq.below: Below T_c: vapour pressure initially rises as volume decreases. Condensation begins at G. Between G and L, liquid and vapour coexist; volume decreases while pressure stays at saturation. At L all material is liquid; further compression raises pressure steeply.
strings.liq.critical: At T_c: the coexistence segment shrinks to the critical point C. Liquid and vapour densities become equal and the interface disappears. The critical isotherm has a horizontal inflection at C.
strings.liq.above: Above T_c: there is no liquefaction plateau. Increasing pressure alone does not produce separate liquid and gas phases. At T > T_c and p > p_c the substance is a supercritical fluid; increasing pressure causes a continuous change.
strings.liq.reference: For CO₂: T_c ≈ 304.13 K = 30.98 °C and p_c ≈ 7.38 MPa. Thus CO₂ can be liquefied by isothermal compression at 20 °C but not at 40 °C. These critical values are physical references; the demonstration curves are a qualitative model.
strings.liq.practice: Liquefaction plants combine compression, heat exchange and cooling in ways suited to the gas. Condensation, evaporation and phase diagrams describe the same liquid–vapour boundary from different perspectives.
strings.liq.lever.title: How much liquid has formed?
strings.liq.lever: In the mixture the liquid mole fraction x_l follows the lever rule. V is the total volume; V_l and V_g are the volumes the same total amount would occupy as saturated liquid and saturated vapour. All volumes must use the same unit.
strings.liq.demo.title: Demo · isothermal compression and liquefaction
strings.liq.demo.hint: Reduce volume below T_c and follow the G–L plateau. Repeat above T_c: pressure rises continuously. Critical point selects C itself. L and G mark the saturated liquid and saturated vapour limits.
strings.liq.diagram.piston: A fixed amount of substance in a piston cylinder
strings.liq.diagram.constant: Constant T · schematic drawing, not to scale
strings.liq.envelope: The dotted boundary joins subcritical plateau endpoints: saturated liquid on the left and saturated vapour on the right. The branches meet at their maximum C. Isotherms at −10, 0, 10, 20, 25 and 29 °C show the plateau shortening and vanishing at T_c ≈ 30.98 °C.
strings.liq.regions: The four regions are: 1 — liquid; 2 — liquid–vapour mixture inside the dotted boundary; 3 — vapour, outside the dotted boundary and below the critical isotherm, at T < T_c; 4 — gas, above the critical isotherm, at T > T_c. Vapour can be liquefied by isothermal compression. Gas at T > T_c cannot be liquefied by compression alone at any pressure: it must first be cooled below T_c. The vapour–gas distinction depends on temperature, not simply on comparing p with p_c. Above both T_c and p_c the term supercritical fluid applies; this four-region classification does not introduce an additional phase boundary there.
strings.liq.volume.scale: Volume uses a logarithmic scale up to about 2.57 L: equal axis intervals represent equal volume ratios. Pressure uses a linear scale. This keeps both the peak and the right-hand saturation branch visible.
strings.liq.scale: Scale for 1 mol: p_c = 7.377 MPa; V_c ≈ 0.129 L; T_c ≈ 30.98 °C. The critical volume is the van der Waals model value, V_c = 3RT_c/(8p_c), not an experimental CO₂ value.
strings.liq.history.title: Milestones in gas liquefaction
strings.liq.history.critical.note: The critical temperature T_c is the upper limit for liquefaction by isothermal compression; it is not a temperature defined at 1 atm. Values are approximate. Hydrogen consistently uses normal hydrogen: boiling at 20.369 K and T_c = 33.145 K; ortho/para forms have slightly different values.
strings.liq.history.source.critical.cryogens: REFPROP critical constants: nitrogen and oxygen
strings.liq.history.source.critical.hydrogen: NIST REFPROP: normal hydrogen, boiling and critical point
strings.liq.history.source.critical.helium: NIST: helium equation of state and critical point
strings.liq.history.pressure: Approximate normal boiling temperatures at standard atmospheric pressure: 1 atm = 101,325 Pa.
strings.liq.history.co2.exception: * CO₂ has no boiling point at 1 atm: under these conditions it sublimes at about −78.5 °C (194.7 K). Liquid can exist only above the triple-point pressure, about 5.1 atm.
strings.liq.history.note: The table lists experimental milestones, not industrial production. Cailletet and Pictet worked independently on oxygen in 1877; in 1883 Wróblewski and Olszewski obtained oxygen and nitrogen as stable liquids with a visible interface. This distinguishes transient condensation from collecting a liquid.

strings.liq.model: The internal calculation uses reduced variables and a van der Waals model with an equilibrium plateau obtained by Maxwell’s construction. ex1511.t: Stage 1 — heating the ice, no change of state

ex1511.n: The temperature does not rise at all over this interval, although the system receives heat.
Melting consumes about 43% of the total heat without increasing temperature.

ex1521.t: What happens inside the evacuated enclosure
ex1521.n: In a simplified adiabatic model, vaporising part of the drop uses the heat released by freezing the remainder. Heat exchange with the vessel and subsequent sublimation are neglected.

ex1521.t: Let f be the fraction of the drop that freezes
The calorimetric equation, in modulus |Q_c| = Q_p
ex1521.n: Mass cancels. The processes are approximated at 0 °C near the triple point. In a continuously evacuated chamber, three-phase coexistence is not a permanent equilibrium.
At 0 °C the latent heat of vaporisation is approximately 2.50 MJ/kg; 2.83 MJ/kg is the latent heat of sublimation.

text.q: What happens to the temperature of a crystalline substance while it melts, at constant pressure?
opts: It rises slowly
It stays constant
It decreases slightly
It depends on the specific heat
text.why: The heat received is spent on breaking the lattice bonds, so the average kinetic energy — and the temperature — do not change.

text.q: What distinguishes a crystalline substance from an amorphous one (pitch) when melting?
opts: The amorphous one absorbs no heat
The crystalline one softens gradually
The amorphous one has no precise melting temperature
The crystalline one boils before melting
text.why: Amorphous substances soften gradually and become more and more fluid as the temperature rises; they have no melting point.

text.q: How much heat Q is needed to turn 100 g of ice at −10 °C into water at 100 °C? (c_g = 2090 J/(kg·K), λ_t = 3.35·10⁵ J/kg, c_a = 4181 J/(kg·K))
How much heat is needed to melt 2 kg of ice completely at 0 °C? (λ_t = 334 kJ/kg)
text.why: Q = λ_t · m = 334 · 2 = 668 kJ, about 16 times more than what is needed to warm 2 kg of ice by 10 K.

text.q: What happens to the volume of ice when it melts?
opts: It grows and the density falls
It shrinks and the density grows
It stays the same
It depends on the atmospheric pressure
text.why: Ice is an exception: ρ_ice = 917 kg/m³, ρ_water = 1000 kg/m³. That is why a higher pressure lowers the melting temperature of ice.

text.q: Which is the defining relation of the specific latent heat of vaporisation?
opts: λ_v = Q·m
λ_v = Q/m
λ_v = m/Q
λ_v = Q·m²
text.why: λ_v = Q/m, hence Q = λ_v · m, with [λ_v] = J/kg. Vaporisation absorbs heat, condensation releases the same heat in modulus.

text.q: In the barometric-tube experiment, what happens to the saturated-vapour pressure if more ether is injected than needed?
opts: It grows proportionally with the amount
It stays equal to p_m and the excess remains liquid
It falls, because the liquid takes up volume
It depends on the mass of vapour in the tube
text.why: p_m depends neither on the mass of liquid nor on the mass of vapour in contact with it.

text.q: At constant temperature the volume above the liquid is increased. What happens to the saturated-vapour pressure?
opts: It falls, following Boyle–Mariotte
It grows
It stays unchanged
It depends on the nature of the liquid
text.why: The larger volume makes an extra amount of liquid vaporise (and vice versa), but the level of the mercury column does not change.

text.q: Why does a liquid cool down while evaporating, without being cooled from outside?
opts: Because the vapour „carries cold”
Because the molecules that leave have kinetic energies above the average
Because the cohesion forces vanish
Because the atmospheric pressure grows
text.why: The fastest molecules leave the liquid, so the average kinetic energy of the remaining ones — and the temperature — drops.

text.q: When does a liquid start to boil?
opts: When the temperature reaches 100 °C
When its saturated-vapour pressure equals the external pressure
When all the liquid has turned into vapour
When the latent heat becomes zero
text.why: The condition is p_saturated(T_boiling) = p_external; that is why water boils at 100 °C at 760 torr but at 0 °C at 4.5 torr.

text.q: At what temperature does water boil when the external pressure is 4.5 torr?
text.why: Exactly at 0 °C: p_sat(0 °C) ≈ 4.54 torr. That is why, in the syringe experiment, room-temperature water starts boiling again.

text.q: A water drop at 0 °C is placed inside an evacuated enclosure. What fraction f freezes? Use λ_v = 2.50·10⁶ J/kg and λ_g = 3.34·10⁵ J/kg.
text.why: f = 2.50/(2.50 + 0.334) ≈ 0.882. Use water’s vaporisation heat at 0 °C, not its sublimation heat.

text.q: What does the triple point of water represent?
opts: The state where ice, water and vapour coexist
The boiling temperature at normal pressure
The point where the vapour pressure is zero
The fastest possible melting
text.why: It is the unique state in which the substance coexists in all three states of aggregation: 273.16 K and p_tr ≈ 611 Pa (4.58 torr).

text.q: Can a gas at T > T_c be liquefied by pressure alone while temperature is held constant?
opts: Yes, once p exceeds p_c
No; isothermal liquefaction requires cooling below T_c first
Yes, if volume is large enough
text.why: Above critical temperature there is no liquid–vapour boundary along an isotherm. Compression gives a continuous change; pressure alone does not liquefy the gas.

text.q: During compression on the plateau of an Andrews isotherm below critical temperature, what happens?
opts: Volume decreases and the liquid fraction grows at constant T and p
Temperature rises while the amount of vapour stays constant
Pressure rises without any liquid forming
text.why: Between G and L, liquid and vapour coexist. Condensation reduces volume at the saturation pressure and imposed temperature; heat must be removed.

answers.ex1511: Q = 77,300 J (77.3 kJ), with λ_t = 334 kJ/kg.
answers.ex1521: f = λ_v/(λ_g + λ_v) ≈ 0.882: approximately 88.2% freezes and 11.8% vaporises.
